name: Functional Inorganic Materials Lab
tagline: We make new chalcogenide crystals, solve their structures, and find out what they can do.
subtitle: Synthesis of new semiconductors and quantum materials
welcome: Our projects span infrared nonlinear optics, capturing heavy metals from water, and two-dimensional magnetism.

showcase.label: New structures
showcase.text: Compounds no one has made before, such as noncentrosymmetric Sr<sub>3</sub>As<sub>2</sub>S<sub>7</sub>.

showcase.label: High-temperature reactions
showcase.text: Elements sealed in silica tubes and heated to 700 °C and beyond.

showcase.label: Crystals
showcase.text: Single crystals grown by flux and chemical vapor transport.

showcase.label: Machine learning
showcase.text: A second route to new compounds: models that suggest what to make and predict properties such as band gaps before synthesis.

address: Room 550, Department of Chemistry, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, MB R3T 2N2, Canada
research_intro: Only a small fraction of chemically possible inorganic compounds has ever been made. We make new ones and work out the crystal-chemical rules that govern how they form and what they can do.

areas.title: Materials discovery and crystal growth
areas.text: Finding new chalcogenides and growing them as large, high-quality single crystals for property measurements.

areas.title: Infrared nonlinear optics
areas.text: Noncentrosymmetric chalcogenides and mixed-anion materials for infrared frequency conversion, lasers, sensing and photonics.

areas.title: Water remediation
areas.text: Metal chalcogenides and hybrids that capture toxic heavy metals from water, and how structure and bonding control their selectivity.

areas.title: Two-dimensional quantum materials
areas.text: Low-dimensional chalcogenides where substitution, intercalation and structural control open up 2D magnetism and correlated electrons.

methods.title: High-temperature synthesis
methods.text: We make metal chalcogenides and mixed-anion materials by sealing the elements in evacuated silica tubes and heating them to as high as about 1100 °C. For two-dimensional layered materials we use chemical vapor transport, where a transport agent such as iodine carries material as a gas along a temperature gradient and deposits it as large single crystals.

methods.title: Flux synthesis
methods.text: We use many different fluxes to reach new phases that are otherwise difficult to obtain. Reactive fluxes such as P<sub>2</sub>S<sub>5</sub> and P<sub>2</sub>Se<sub>5</sub> build complex chalcogenide frameworks, while non-reactive halide and polychalcogenide fluxes let new crystals grow at lower temperatures and give us access to phases that direct reactions miss.

methods.title: AI-guided discovery
methods.text: Machine learning combined with crystal chemistry and computational modelling predicts which compounds to make next. Through active learning, every experimental result, including failed reactions, is fed back into our models, so each round of synthesis makes the next set of predictions stronger.

equipment.title: Sealing a reaction tube
equipment.text: Reactants are sealed inside a silica tube under vacuum with a torch, ready for the furnace.

equipment.title: Vacuum line
equipment.text: A stainless-steel manifold and pump evacuate the tubes before sealing, so reactions run without air or moisture.

equipment.title: Two-zone tube furnace
equipment.text: Two independently controlled zones set up the temperature gradient for growing crystals by chemical vapor transport.

equipment.title: Box furnaces
equipment.text: Programmable furnaces run solid-state and flux reactions, often for days at a time.

equipment.title: Muffle furnace
equipment.text: Heats samples in air for annealing and preparing starting materials.

openings_intro: No research experience needed to start. You learn by doing: making new compounds with your own hands, solving their structures, and finding out what they can do.

openings.text: Most students start in second or third year. There are three ways in:
steps: CHEM 4710 honours project (fall and winter terms)
NSERC USRA summer research award (applications are usually due in winter for the following summer)
openings.send: Your CV, an unofficial transcript, and a few lines on what interests you.

openings.text: We look for curiosity about inorganic and structural chemistry. A strong cover letter and hands-on research experience in materials, inorganic or solid-state chemistry, or engineering matter more than grades alone.
steps: Email Abishek first to talk about projects and funding
Apply through the UManitoba graduate program in Chemistry
Ask about fellowships such as NSERC CGS-M and the UM Graduate Fellowship
openings.send: Your CV, transcripts, and a short statement of your research interests.

openings.text: Candidates should have experience characterizing solids and a record of publishing research articles. Applicants with their own funding, such as an NSERC or Banting fellowship, are welcome.
steps: Email Abishek to discuss a project idea
Plan a fellowship application together if you are applying for your own funding
openings.send: Your CV, a short research statement, and contact details for two referees.

week.title: In the lab
week.text: Most of the week is hands-on: preparing reactions, running furnaces, picking crystals and collecting X-ray data, with a postdoc or senior student nearby to help.

week.title: Group meeting
week.text: Every week we share results, practise talks, and work through problems together.

week.title: One-on-one with Abishek
week.text: Regular meetings to look at your data, plan the next experiments, and talk about your goals.

week.title: Conferences
week.text: Students present their own work at meetings such as the Canadian Chemistry Conference and the North American Solid State Chemistry Conference.

week.title: Group life
week.text: Dinners, celebrations and end-of-summer get-togethers with the solid-state groups at UManitoba.

highlights.label: Infrared photonics
highlights.title: A new family of infrared optical materials
highlights.text: The first major discovery from the Iyer Lab. We made the first chalcoarsenate semiconductors in which As<sup>3+</sup> and As<sup>5+</sup> coexist, and showed that engineering arsenic coordination switches on one of the strongest nonlinear optical responses in this class of materials. The work sets out a new crystal-chemical design strategy for infrared photonics and was characterized with collaborators in South Korea. It was co-authored by lab members Vidyanshu Mishra and Manya Rishi (NSERC USRA).
highlights.role: Corresponding author · from the Iyer Lab

highlights.label: Infrared lasers
highlights.title: About 20 times the commercial benchmark
highlights.text: A new synthetic route produced high-quality single crystals of γ-NaAs<sub>0.95</sub>Sb<sub>0.05</sub>Se<sub>2</sub>, one of the highest-performing infrared nonlinear optical semiconductors reported. Its response is about twenty times that of the commercial benchmark AgGaSe<sub>2</sub>.

highlights.label: Clean water
highlights.title: How lead and cadmium are captured from acidic water
highlights.text: Crystallography and kinetic studies uncovered a previously unknown mechanism for the selective removal of toxic lead and cadmium by an ion-exchange material. The findings give design rules for better remediation materials and inspired the lab's AI-driven water remediation program in Manitoba.
highlights.citation: Pournara et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society 2026

vision: Our long-term goal is to turn inorganic materials discovery from trial and error into a predictive science. By combining data-driven design with experimental validation, we aim to find materials for infrared photonics, advanced semiconductors, quantum technologies and sustainable water remediation, while training scientists who are fluent in synthesis, crystallography, modelling and machine learning.
